Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝑿i)+ϵi,f(𝒙)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.
Show the workflow 
set.seed(43251)
x0 <- c(0.5, 0.7, 1)
k_values <- seq(1, 29, by = 2)
f <- function(x1, x2, x3) 0.5 * x1 + sin(x2) - 0.3 * x3^2

f_x0 <- f(x0[1], x0[2], x0[3])

knn_predict_x0 <- function(X, y, x0, k_values) {
  d <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, x0, "-")^2))
  y_sorted <- y[order(d)]
  sapply(k_values, function(k) mean (y_sorted[1:k]))
}

  1. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Show the workflow 
n_sim <- 200
pred_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_sim, ncol = length(k_values))

for (i in 1:n_sim) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n, ncol = 3)
  y <- f(X[, 1], X[, 2], X[, 3]) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
  pred_matrix[i, ] <- knn_predict_x0(X, y, x0, k_values)
}

bias <- colMeans(pred_matrix) - f_x0
variance <- colMeans((sweep(pred_matrix, 2, colMeans(pred_matrix), "-"))^2)
mse <- colMeans((pred_matrix - f_x0)^2)

all.equal(mse, bias^2 + variance)
[1] TRUE

When the k is small, each prediction uses a few nearby responses, so it has low bias from the local mean, but a high variance because of how much the a few noisy observations can change the prediction. As k gets bigger, bias increases and variance increases. This is because points further from the target point are being used, allowing for the local mean to not be represented.

A small k acts as a small penalty and a large k acts as a large penalty. This is similar to the bias-variance tradeoff of LASSO and ridge regression, except the penalty isn’t applied to the coeffcieints in KNN. Instead, the penalty is applied to the number of neighbors used in a prediction. A small k allows for a more flexible model, while a large k forces the model to be more rigid.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝑿∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

Used AI for this code.

Show the workflow 
library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 5.0
Show the workflow 
set.seed(43252)

n_train <- 400
n_test <- 1000
p <- 30
lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 41)
lambda_dec <- sort(lambda_grid, decreasing = TRUE)

f <- function(X) 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2

# Setting 1: independent covariates.
# Setting 2: pairwise correlation 0.8, built from one shared factor
# plus independent noise for each covariate.
gen_X <- function(n, setting) {
  if (setting == 1) {
    matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
  } else {
    common <- rnorm(n)
    sqrt(0.8) * matrix(common, nrow = n, ncol = p) +
      sqrt(0.2) * matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
  }
}

gen_data <- function(setting) {
  Xtr <- gen_X(n_train, setting)
  ytr <- f(Xtr) + rnorm(n_train, sd = 0.1)
  Xte <- gen_X(n_test, setting)
  yte <- f(Xte) + rnorm(n_test, sd = 0.1)
  list(Xtr = Xtr, ytr = ytr, Xte = Xte, yte = yte)
}

# 5NN with Euclidean distance on the supplied scale
knn_predict <- function(Xtr, ytr, Xte, k = 5) {
  d2 <- outer(rowSums(Xte^2), rowSums(Xtr^2), "+") - 2 * Xte %*% t(Xtr)
  apply(d2, 1, function(row) mean(ytr[order(row)[1:k]]))
}

# Lasso: means and scales come only from the data passed to each fit
standardize_fit <- function(X) {
  list(mean = colMeans(X),
       sd = apply(X, 2, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - mean(col))^2))))
}
apply_std <- function(X, st) sweep(sweep(X, 2, st$mean, "-"), 2, st$sd, "/")

fit_lasso <- function(X, y, lambdas) {
  st <- standardize_fit(X)
  Xs <- apply_std(X, st)
  fit <- glmnet(Xs, y - mean(y), alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas, family = gaussian(),
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE,
                control = list(thresh = 1e-14, maxit = 1000000))
  list(beta = as.matrix(fit$beta), st = st, ybar = mean(y))
}

predict_lasso <- function(obj, Xnew) {
  obj$ybar + apply_std(Xnew, obj$st) %*% obj$beta
}

cv_lasso <- function(X, y, lambdas, K = 10) {
  folds <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(X)))
  err <- matrix(NA, nrow = K, ncol = length(lambdas))
  for (fold in 1:K) {
    idx <- folds == fold
    obj <- fit_lasso(X[!idx, , drop = FALSE], y[!idx], lambdas)
    pred <- predict_lasso(obj, X[idx, , drop = FALSE])
    err[fold, ] <- colMeans((y[idx] - pred)^2)
  }
  colMeans(err)
}

run_setting <- function(setting) {
  dat <- gen_data(setting)
  knn_mse <- mean((dat$yte - knn_predict(dat$Xtr, dat$ytr, dat$Xte, k = 5))^2)
  cv_err <- cv_lasso(dat$Xtr, dat$ytr, lambda_dec)
  best <- which.min(cv_err)
  obj <- fit_lasso(dat$Xtr, dat$ytr, lambda_dec[best])
  lasso_mse <- mean((dat$yte - predict_lasso(obj, dat$Xte))^2)
  data.frame(setting = setting, knn_mse = knn_mse, lasso_mse = lasso_mse,
             lasso_lambda = lambda_dec[best], nonzero_slopes = sum(abs(obj$beta) > 1e-8))
}

results <- rbind(run_setting(1), run_setting(2))
results
  setting   knn_mse lasso_mse lasso_lambda nonzero_slopes
1       1 0.5681199 0.2866887   0.03981072              5
2       2 0.1799867 0.2321411   0.01584893              8

Used seed 43252. The numbers are in order of knn_mse, lasso_mse, lasso_lambda, nonzero_slopes. Setting 1 has the results of 0.568, 0.287, 0.0398, 5. Setting 2 has the results of 0.18, 0.232, 0.0158, 8.

  1. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

KNN improved a lot from setting 1 to setting 2 because the test mse falls from 0.568 to 0.18 while the lasso mse didn’t fall that much. We conclude with correlated covariates, KNN is the better method.

When covariates are correlated, the Euclidean distance between observations may not accurately reflect their similarity in terms of the underlying relationship with the response variable. This is because correlated covariated are largely affected by the same factor, whereas independent covariates, many of them do not have anything to do with the response variable.

Lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN because KNN gives all the covariates equal weight in the distance and doesn’t look at the response when choosing neighbors. Lasso uses the response to learn a weight for each covariate so it can drop irrelevant covariates. In our example, the Lasso nonzero slopes are 5 and 8 for the two settings, which is significantly less than the 30 covariates available.

  1. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

The lasso fit uses only linear terms, which means it cannot capture the nonlinear relationships present in the true response model, specifically the sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2 terms. This limitation can lead to a poorer fit and higher test MSE for lasso compared to KNN, which can adapt to nonlinear relationships through its local averaging of neighbors.

These results would not justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN or that one method is always better. Things like the choice of k and correlation level can affect the performance of KNN. A truly linear response would heavily favor lasso, and a correlation structure that spreads the signal across many directions instead of one shared facor could hurt KNN rather than help. The comparison shows that the outcome depends on the interaction between model form and the geometry of the covariates.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i+𝜼i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝑨∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝒁i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝜼i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝑨\mathbf A. Generate 𝑨\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝑿\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝒁\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

Show the workflow 
set.seed(43253)

p <- 100
n_train <- 200
n_test <- 200
k_values <- seq(2, 82, by = 8)
m_values <- c(3, 30)

gen_data <- function(m) {
  A <- matrix(runif(p * m, -2, 2), nrow = p, ncol = m)
  make_part <- function(n) {
    Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * m), nrow = n, ncol = m)
    eta <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
    X <- Z %*% t(A) + eta
    y <- Z[, 1] + Z[, 2] + rnorm(n)
    list(X = X, y = y)
  }
  list(train = make_part(n_train), test = make_part(n_test))
}

knn_test_mse <- function(dat, k_values) {
  Xtr <- dat$train$X; ytr <- dat$train$y
  Xte <- dat$test$X;  yte <- dat$test$y
  d2 <- outer(rowSums(Xte^2), rowSums(Xtr^2), "+") - 2 * Xte %*% t(Xtr)
  sq_err <- sapply(1:nrow(Xte), function(i) {
    y_sorted <- ytr[order(d2[i, ])]
    cum_mean <- cumsum(y_sorted) / seq_along(y_sorted)
    (yte[i] - cum_mean[k_values])^2
  })
  rowMeans(sq_err)
}
  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

Averaged over 50 repetitions, the m = 3 curve sits well below the m = 30 curve at every k. The best average test MSE is about 1.30 for m = 3 (at k = 10) and about 2.33 for m = 30 (at k = 18), a gap of roughly one full unit. Both curves are highest at k = 2 (1.66 and 3.01), where each prediction relies on only two noisy responses, are lowest at a moderate k, and then rise slowly as the neighborhood grows and starts to include less similar observations. The noise in Y has variance 1, so no method can get below a test MSE of 1. The best m = 3 result is about 0.3 above that floor, while the best m = 30 result is more than 1.3 above it.

  1. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

The two settings have the same number of observed covariates (100) and the same response, which depends on only two latent variables, yet KNN does much better when m = 3. What matters is not the number of measured covariates but how many latent directions the observed covariates vary along. KNN measures similarity using all 100 coordinates of X, so two observations are near each other when their whole latent vectors are near each other. When m = 3, being close in X means being close in three latent variables, and two of those are exactly the ones that determine Y, so the neighbors have similar responses. When m = 30, being close in X requires being close in 30 latent variables, and 28 of them have nothing to do with Y. With only 200 training points, the nearest neighbors are far apart in the 30-dimensional latent space, so they are typically not close in the two variables that matter, and the neighbors’ responses differ from the target. This is the curse of dimensionality operating on the latent dimension: the data have a hidden lower-dimensional structure, and how low that dimension is determines how well local averaging works.

The noise eta plays two roles. First, it adds independent variation in all 100 coordinates, so the squared distance between any two observations contains a large noise contribution (about 200 on average, from 100 coordinates with variance 1 each for two observations) that has nothing to do with Y. This blurs the distance and makes the nearest neighbors less reliable, in both settings. Second, it means the observed data are not confined exactly to an m-dimensional linear space. Without eta, every X would be exactly A Z, a combination of the m columns of A, and would lie precisely in an m-dimensional linear subspace of the 100-dimensional space. With eta, each X is displaced off that subspace by independent noise in every one of the 100 directions, so the data lie near the m-dimensional subspace but fill a small band of thickness one around it in all the remaining directions. The signal is much larger than the noise along the m latent directions, so the low-dimensional structure is still visible in the data, and that is why KNN can work in the m = 3 case, but it is not exact, and the noise directions add distance without adding information about Y.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. The package has been retired from the active CRAN repository. If needed, install the archived package into your usual R library, then load the two datasets. Python users can use the course copies of the same training data and test data. These compressed CSV files have no headers and are included in the homework ZIP under data/knn. Run the Python code from the folder containing data.

Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝒙i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

Show the workflow 
train_raw <- read.csv("data/knn/zip-train.csv.gz", header = FALSE)
test_raw  <- read.csv("data/knn/zip-test.csv.gz", header = FALSE)

train_y <- train_raw[1:1000, 1]
train_X <- as.matrix(train_raw[1:1000, -1])
test_y  <- test_raw[1:500, 1]
test_X  <- as.matrix(test_raw[1:500, -1])

dim(train_X)
[1] 1000  256
Show the workflow 
dim(test_X)
[1] 500 256
  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.
Show the workflow 
knn5_classify <- function(train_X, train_y, test_X, distance = "euclidean", k = 5) {
  preds <- integer(nrow(test_X))
  for (i in 1:nrow(test_X)) {
    diffs <- sweep(train_X, 2, test_X[i, ], "-")
    d <- if (distance == "euclidean") sqrt(rowSums(diffs^2)) else rowSums(abs(diffs))
    nearest <- order(d)[1:k]   # order() keeps tied distances in original row order
    votes <- table(factor(train_y[nearest], levels = 0:9))
    preds[i] <- as.integer(names(votes)[which.max(votes)])   # first max = smallest digit
  }
  preds
}

The classifier computes the Euclidean distance or the Manhattan distance from a test image to all 1,000 training images, takes the five nearest, and returns the most frequent label among them. Distance ties are broken by the smaller training row number, and voting ties by the smallest digit. The first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test were used, with the original pixel values and no standardization.

Test classification error with Euclidean distance was 0.122 (61 of 500 images wrong), and with Manhattan distance it was 0.138 (69 of 500 wrong). The confusion matrices, with predicted digits in rows and true digits in columns, are shown above and include all digits 0 through 9.

The most common confusion for Euclidean distance was true 2 predicted as 0 (7 times), followed by four confusions with 4 cases each: true 5 predicted as 0, true 5 predicted as 3, true 4 predicted as 9, and true 9 predicted as 7. True 2 predicted as 8 came next (3 times). Manhattan distance shows a similar pattern: true 2 predicted as 0 (6 times), true 9 predicted as 7 and true 5 predicted as 0 (5 times each), then true 5 predicted as 3, true 4 predicted as 9, and true 8 predicted as 0 (4 times each). Digit 5 is the hardest digit for both methods, with only 13 of its 26 test images classified correctly under Euclidean distance and 11 under Manhattan distance. The confused pairs are digits whose handwritten shapes overlap: 4 and 9 share a similar upper part, 9 and 7 share a vertical stroke with a top bar, 5 and 3 share a similar lower curve, and 2 and 0 can both be drawn with a large rounded loop.

The three misclassified images shown above have true labels 6, 2 and 4, and were predicted as 0, 0 and 7. Each pairing is understandable. A 6 has a rounded loop in its lower half, so if the upper stroke is short or faint, the image looks like a 0. A 2 written with a large rounded curve and a weak bottom stroke can look like a 0 as well, and this was also the most common confusion in the Euclidean confusion matrix (true 2 predicted as 0, 7 times). A 4 with an open top, or one where the diagonal stroke is more prominent than the vertical one, can look like a 7. Most of these mistakes are ones a person reading messy handwriting could also make. The neighbors are genuinely similar in pixel space, but similar pixel patterns do not always mean the same digit.

The two distances can have similar total error while making mistakes on different images, and in this run they do. Euclidean distance had 61 errors and Manhattan distance had 69, a difference of 8 images or 1.6 percentage points. But the two classifiers gave different predictions on 22 of the 500 test images. Of the 61 Euclidean errors, 58 were also Manhattan errors, 3 were Euclidean-only errors, and 11 were Manhattan-only errors, so 14 images were misclassified by exactly one of the two distances. The other 8 disagreements were images that both classifiers got wrong but with different predicted digits. So similar total error does not mean the same mistakes: the two distances rank the neighbors differently, because Euclidean distance squares each pixel difference and so weights a few large pixel differences more heavily, while Manhattan distance weights all pixel differences in proportion to their size. A different set of five neighbors can produce a different vote for an individual image even when the overall error rate comes out close. With only 500 test images, the 8-image gap between the two methods is small enough that I would not claim Euclidean distance is better in general from this one comparison.
